spans.assertion: a mixed-effects model was used to test whether darker player skin tone had a systematic impact on likelihood of penalization
standard regression procedures such as OLS were judged unsuitable because they would likely yield incorrect coefficients given the highly non-normal dependent variable
a zero-inflated Poisson model was used to determine the impact of skin color on receiving red cards
the analysis found a slim (p < .10) interaction effect between skin color and referee-country implicit bias on red card issuance
no direct effect of skin color itself on red card issuance was found
there is a significant (p < .10) relationship among player skin color, referee-country implicit racial bias, and red card issuance

spans.assertion: an OLS approach was ruled out because it assumes normality of the dependent variable, which does not hold here
the data were found to contain far more zero counts than a standard Poisson distribution can account for

spans.note: general explanation of hurdle vs. zero-inflated mixture distributions

spans.assertion: a zero-inflated distribution (rather than a hurdle distribution) was used in this analysis

spans.note: notes that the dual-coefficient structure of the model makes interpretation harder

spans.assertion: reported regression coefficients are taken from the binomial zero-inflated portion of the model rather than the count portion
cases without skin color ratings were removed from the dataset
the dependent variable was defined as the number of red cards given in a referee-player dyad
the primary predictor of interest was the focal player's skin color
the skin color variable was created by averaging the two raters' ratings
skin color was treated as a continuous variable
secondary predictors were mean implicit and explicit bias in the referee's country of origin
player weight was included as a control, under the assumption that heavier players appear more physical and thus draw more penalization
player position was included as a control to address differing penalty propensities between defensive and offensive roles
number of games played was included as a control for differing exposure across dyads

spans.note: caveat about theoretical ambiguity of the games-played control, with citation to Harrison et al. 2002

spans.assertion: two models were fit for interpretation: one with main effects only, and one adding interactions between skin color and the two bias predictors

spans.note: repeated page header and blank lines

spans.assertion: Model 1 found no support for skin color affecting the quantity of red cards received (-0.030, ns)
Model 2 found a marginally significant skin color × implicit bias interaction (11.763, p < .10)
Model 2 found no significant skin color × explicit bias interaction (-1.431, ns)
feedback on the initial approach identified a need to address nesting of observations by referee
several mixed-effects models (Poisson and binomial) were attempted
all attempted mixed-effects models failed to converge
dummy codes for referee were used in the ZIP regression as a conservative alternative to a mixed-effects model
the dummy-code approach accounts for systematic referee fixed effects but is less efficient (costs more degrees of freedom) than a true mixed-effects model
the same variables were reused in the final approach, except the skin color variable was rescaled to a 0-1 continuous variable
Model 3 found no support for a direct effect of skin color on red carding (-0.119, ns)
Model 4 found a marginally significant skin color × implicit bias interaction (45.090, p < .10)
Model 4 found no significant skin color × explicit bias interaction (-5.334, ns)
the results are interpreted as showing that player race has no impact on red card issuance
the results are interpreted as showing that referee implicit bias does impact red card issuance
the overall conclusion is that player skin color is not categorically associated with higher penalization, except when the referee is from a country with higher implicit racial bias
a more standard OLS approach was additionally attempted by the author as a check
that OLS approach would indicate a large and significant effect of player skin color on red card receipt
the discrepancy between the OLS and ZIP results is taken to show the results are sensitive to the analytical assumptions used
